fieldData.guide-section-heading: Influencer marketing for small business: a guide
fieldData.guide-section-content:
What influencer marketing involves for a small business

You pick creators whose followers look like your customers, agree what they'll make and what you'll give them, review the content, then pay. For a small business that can mean one creator and one post. There are three common ways to pay:

  • Product gifting. You send the product and the creator decides whether to post. Many creators will also ask for a fee, so say in your brief what you're offering.
  • Commission. The creator gets a code or link and earns a share of the sales it brings in.
  • A flat fee. You pay a set amount for a post or video.

You can combine them, for example a fee plus a code.

What influencer marketing costs a small business

There's no single price. Rates depend on the creator's followers, platform, deliverables and usage rights. The FAQ on Jem Social's Influencer Rate Calculator page lists typical rates per Instagram post: $100 to $500 for nano creators (1,000 to 10,000 followers), $500 to $3,000 for micro creators (10,000 to 100,000) and $3,000 to $15,000 for macro creators (100,000 to 1 million). It says TikTok rates run slightly lower and that usage rights add to the base rate. These are estimates, not quotes, and each creator sets their own price.

On a small budget, those figures mean you can book several smaller creators for what one larger creator charges. Put your budget in the brief, ask each creator for a rate and the deliverables, and agree on usage rights before any content is made. Reusing the content as ads usually costs more.

See how Jem Social's price compares with 7 other platforms, or read our comparison of influencer platforms for small businesses.

How to choose creators on a small budget

  • Customers first. Pick creators whose followers look like your customers and who are based where you sell.
  • Engagement for their size. Compare creators in the same follower range, not against the whole market. The Engagement Rate Calculator works it out from any public profile.
  • Recent content. Look at their latest posts. Is it the quality you'd run in your own ads?
  • Past brand deals. Check how the creator disclosed them and whether the content fits your brand.
  • A real following. Look for steady follower growth, comments from real people, and posts that match what the creator says they do.
  • A way to track results. Give each creator their own code or link so you can see which posts led to sales.

Disclosure

The FTC says an endorsement should make it obvious when the creator has a relationship with the brand, including when they got free products. The disclosure should sit with the endorsement itself, not only on a profile page or behind a "more" link. (FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers, checked November 17, 2026.) Put it in your brief. Each platform also has its own label: see our Instagram guide and TikTok guide. This is general information, not legal advice.

Running your first campaign

  1. Write a brief: the product, deliverables, talking points, budget and deadline. The Campaign Brief Generator gives you a template.
  2. Post it as a free brief on Jem Social, or search creators and message them.
  3. Agree on the rate, deliverables, usage rights and how the creator will disclose the partnership.
  4. Review the content. Payment is released once you approve it.
  5. Track the results with each creator's code or link, and measure them with the Influencer Marketing ROI Calculator.

fieldData.why-section-heading: Why influencer marketing works for small business budgets.
fieldData.why-section-description: Small business budgets demand authentic creator partnerships, not celebrity-tier deals. Nano and micro influencers deliver high engagement at affordable rates — when you can source them efficiently. Jem Social filters creators by budget, niche, and engagement so small businesses run high-ROI campaigns without overpaying or wasting weeks on outreach.
fieldData.why-card-1-description: Small business influencer marketing often builds stronger audience relationships because creator content feels native, on-niche, and community-aware — unlike traditional ads.
fieldData.why-card-2-description: Most small business influencer marketing programs are easier to test than large media buys, making them useful for controlled experiments before committing significant budget.
fieldData.why-card-3-description: Small business influencer marketing can help brands reach buyers through trusted recommendations, niche authority, and engaged audience pockets that broad ad campaigns miss.
fieldData.why-card-4-description: From outreach to published content, small business influencer marketing campaigns can move quickly when the brief, offer, and creator partnerships are clear from the start.
